title: One-year spikes in other pay
question: Which employees received other pay in one year that was many times their own usual level, and was it a payout on leaving or something that happened in mid-career?
finding: Of 27,654 employees who can be followed for four years or more, 242 had at least one year in which other pay was five times their usual level and $50,000 or more above it (291 such years, $25.1 million): it is uncommon. 135 of the years were on leaving ($12.0 million), 70 were followed by more work ($5.9 million) and 86 are in fiscal 2026, too recent to tell. The mid-career ones are concentrated: 52 of the 70 are in Police, 63 of the 70 fall in fiscal 2023 to 2025, and the commonest classes are Lieutenant 3 (20), Sergeant 3 (16) and Police Officer 3 (10). 33 people have two or more such years, which is a new level of pay rather than a spike. Largest mid-career: $308,317 against a usual $4,017 (a line attorney at the Public Defender, Attorney (Civil/Criminal) (class 8177), fiscal 2023). Largest on leaving: $325,556 (William Coaker Jr., Chf Executive & Investment Ofc (class 1119), fiscal 2022).
how: City payroll file, fiscal 2017 to 2026. A person is followed only where the name is rare, has one spelling and never holds two full-time jobs at once; each year’s City rows are added up. Usual other pay is the middle value of the person’s other years (at least three). A year is listed when other pay is at least five times that and at least $50,000 above it. “On leaving” means no later year on the payroll, or later years of under half-time hours; “still working afterwards” means a later year of half-time hours or more. One row for each person, showing their largest such year; the table groups them into mid-career cases, the latest year and cases on leaving. Titles are printed as the payroll prints them (Dep is deputy, Chf is chief, Asst is assistant, Sprv is supervisor, Ofc is officer, EMT is emergency medical technician).
limits: A payout on leaving is unused vacation, sick leave and time off in lieu being paid at the end of a career: money already earned, at rates the labour agreements set. A mid-career spike can be the same thing where an agreement allows leave to be cashed in service, or a lump sum under a new agreement, a legal settlement, back pay after a grievance, or a retention payment. The cluster in the police department in fiscal 2023 to 2025 sits beside the agreement the budget analyst described as bringing “wage increases, retention pay, step adjustments, and signing bonus”; the payroll file cannot confirm that this is what the payments were. A person who retired and came back part-time is counted as leaving. The pay codes, which the public file does not carry, would say what each payment was.
